title: Chain of custody: who held it, when, and how it moved
audience: Accessioning archivists, repositories receiving transferred or deposited material
intro: Custody history is usually written as a paragraph of prose - readable by a person, invisible to everything else. It is also the part of a description most often challenged, because authenticity arguments turn on it. This scenario models a transfer between custodians as a first-class event, so the chain can be queried rather than only read.
question: Records passed from a company, to a liquidator, to us. Is that a note on the record, or something I model?

steps.prompt: A defunct company's minute books came to you via its liquidator. Start with the material.

choices.label: Record Set
choices.why: Fits. The minute books arrived and are managed as one body of material, so the Set is what custody attaches to. Individual volumes hang beneath it.

choices.label: Record
choices.why: Too low. A single minute book is a Record; the custody chain you are about to describe applies to the whole accession.

choices.label: Instantiation
choices.why: That is the physical volumes as carriers. Custody does move with carriers, but what you are describing here is the intellectual body of material.

capture.comment: Create the accession as a Record Set.

steps.prompt: The liquidator handed the books to your repository in 2019. How do you model that handover?

choices.label: Activity - a transfer event
choices.why: Fits. A handover is something that happened at a time, in a place, between parties. As an Activity it can carry all of that and be found by a query. This is the move that turns custody from prose into data.

choices.label: A note on the Record Set
choices.why: The traditional answer, and the reason custody is so hard to audit. A note cannot be filtered, cannot be ordered, and cannot say who was on each side of the handover.

choices.label: Rule - the deposit agreement governs it
choices.why: The agreement is a real Rule and worth recording, but it is the instrument authorising the transfer, not the transfer itself. Model both, and do not let one stand in for the other.

capture.comment: Create the 2019 handover as a transfer Activity.
Link the accession to the transfer that brought it in.

steps.prompt: Two parties were involved: the liquidator handing over, and your repository receiving. How do both get recorded?

choices.label: Corporate Body for each, both linked to the transfer
choices.why: Fits. A transfer has at least two sides, and an Activity can relate to several agents. Recording only the receiver loses half the event - and it is the handing-over party that authenticity questions usually turn on.

choices.label: Corporate Body for the repository only
choices.why: Half the story. 'We hold it' is not a custody chain; 'we received it from X on this date' is.

choices.label: Person - the individual liquidator who signed
choices.why: Not wrong so much as too narrow. The signing officer acted for the firm; record the firm, and the individual too if the signature matters evidentially.

capture.comment: Create the liquidator as an Agent.
Record the liquidator as a performer of the transfer.
Record the repository as current holder of the material.

steps.prompt: Before the liquidator, the company itself held the books for forty years. Does that earlier custody need modelling too?

choices.label: Yes - the company is an earlier custodian and a separate relation
choices.why: Fits. Custody is a chain, not a single handover. The creating company held its own records before anyone else did, and that period is part of the provenance even though no transfer event marks its start.

choices.label: No - only transfers into the archive matter
choices.why: A common shortcut that breaks authenticity arguments. Where material was between creation and accession is exactly what a challenge will probe.

choices.label: Yes, but as the same Agent as the liquidator
choices.why: They are different organisations with different interests. Collapsing them hides the moment control changed hands, which is the most consequential point in the chain.

capture.comment: Create the originating company as an Agent.
Record the company as the creator of its own minute books.

steps.prompt: There is a gap: nobody knows where the books were between the company's collapse in 2016 and the liquidator's inventory in 2018. What do you record?

choices.label: Record the gap honestly and assert nothing for those years
choices.why: Fits, and it matters more than it looks. An unbroken chain you cannot evidence is worth less than a documented break. Leaving the period unasserted lets a reader see exactly where the evidence stops - which is what an authenticity assessment needs.

choices.label: Extend the company's custody to 2018 as the likely case
choices.why: Invents evidence. A plausible assumption recorded as a relation is indistinguishable from a documented one two archivists later.

choices.label: Extend the liquidator's custody back to 2016
choices.why: Same problem from the other end. The liquidator was not appointed until 2018; claiming earlier custody asserts something nobody witnessed.

outcome.verdict: A chain you can query, including where it breaks.
outcome.summary: The accession is a Record Set. The 2019 handover is a transfer Activity with both parties attached, not a sentence in a note field. The originating company is recorded as creator and earlier custodian, and the two-year gap is left unasserted rather than smoothed over. You can now ask who held this material in a given year, and get either an answer or an honest silence - which is the distinction that makes a custody chain worth keeping at all.
